- Forced flexion/hyperflexion injury to the DIP joint — classic mechanism for terminal extensor tendon disruption.  
- Progressive pain and swelling localized precisely to the DIP joint — anatomic concordance with extensor tendon insertion.  
- X-rays show no fracture or dislocation but demonstrate soft tissue swelling centered at the DIP joint — typical appearance of acute mallet injury, especially tendinous type.

- Absence of erythema, warmth, purulence, or fever makes infection highly unlikely.  

[GAPS]

- Resting posture of the fingertip (i.e., presence of fixed DIP flexion deformity).  
- Result of “tendon test” (holding PIP in extension while asking patient to extend DIP — failure confirms terminal extensor insufficiency).

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Mallet finger

- **Mechanism:** Forced flexion/hyperflexion injury to the right ring finger DIP joint during football (jersey entanglement and abrupt pull).

The clinical scenario describes a classic mechanism for mallet finger: forced flexion/hyperflexion of the DIP joint — in this case, due to jersey entanglement and abrupt pull during football.
